pr_body:
The conversion from IPv4 string presentation to numeric value did not check if the individual address value was between 0 and 255 inclusive.

Add also test case for this.

Fixes #84593
pr_comments:
I've always been curious as to why these `zsock_inet_pton()` and `zsock_inet_ntop()` were implemented as `__syscall`s. There are no kernel or private resources to synchronize on.

On machines with an mmu or mpu, there would be a fault of reading or writing outside of the allowed addressable memory.

In any case, the only thing I can suggest is to look at some of the degenerate cases such as the one that @pdgendt highlighted. But also, it would be good to cross-reference against e.g. the glibc or musl implementations or picolibc. See what kinds of invalid input those detect and try to match common behaviour.

Ofc, one could technically implement a bunch of exhaustive tests in the POSIX test suite, but it would be nice if the native Zephyr call were just compliant.

Added more checks (from stackoverflow) and added tests.
Just wondering should we disallow perfectly valid IPv4 addresses like `0`, `1`, `0.0` etc. (so values < 256). Atm we do not support the "plain int" addresses like `2130706433` which is `127.0.0.1`

issue_context.title: Zephyr posix inet_pton incorrect conversions.
issue_context.body:
<!--
**Notes**
Github Discussions (https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/discussions)
are available to first verify that the issue is a genuine Zephyr bug and not a
consequence of Zephyr services misuse.

This issue list is only for bugs in the main Zephyr code base
(https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/). If the bug is for a project
fork (such as NCS) specific feature, please open an issue in the fork project
instead.
-->

**Describe the bug**
Zephyr implementation of inet_pton is probably not working properly for IP v4 addresses.
For example for the ip4 ip string in the format "192.168.1.400", the inet_pton function should return avalue other than 1. 
Instead, inet_pton returns 1 and in the address structure the result ip is malformed.

**To Reproduce**

issue code like below:

```
  struct in_addr addr;
  char stripv4[] = "192.168.1.400";
  int ret = inet_pton(AF_INET, stripv4, &addr);
  if (ret == 1) {
    LOG_INF("Parsed test IP from string: %s to %d.%d.%d.%d", stripv4,
            addr.s4_addr[0], addr.s4_addr[1], addr.s4_addr[2], addr.s4_addr[3]);
  }
```


**Expected behavior**
Log information should not show as the ret value should be different than 1

**Impact**
Instead, log system with minimal logs turned on, presents :
"I: Parsed test IP from string: 192.168.1.400 to 192.168.1.144"
The parsed IP address from the string is incorrect, returned value should be different than 1.

This annoyance involves adding additional sanity checks for IP addresses as they are wrongly parsed from the string.

**Environment (please complete the following information):**

We are using Zephyr 3.7.1

**Additional context**
<!--
Add any other context that could be relevant to your issue, such as pin setting,
target configuration, ...
-->

review_comments:
~~You could move the `index++` here and verify that `index == sizeof(struct in_addr)` after the loop, that way you can remove `count` altogether.~~

EDIT: it's used to assign a value, so scratch that.

Reading the implementation, I think you can easily read beyond the data. If the data is provided from an external source, and for example `"0.0"` is passed, this will call `strtol` with memory after the string (twice).

I might have missed some discussion, but I'm not sure I follow why should these be considered valid IP addresses? Even checked with native Linux app, and they're all rejected by `inet_pton()`:
```
inet_pton returned 0 for 0.0
inet_pton returned 0 for 0.1
inet_pton returned 0 for 0
inet_pton returned 0 for 1
```
I think they probably are not valid IP addresses.
Ok, lets ban these short addresses then. I have seen these used as IP addresses but it probably was not with `inet_pton` but with some other tool.

I do not think they are invalid at all, they may be unusable. Those adresses may be invalid on the public internet or have a designated not "free for all" usage.
The IANA list: https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv4-special-registry/iana-ipv4-special-registry.xhtml for example lists addresses 0.0.0.0 and its subnet as valid but to limited use. 
Maybe we should follow https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/009604499/functions/[inet_ntop](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/009604499/functions/inet_ntop.html).html
so an adress like 0.0 will be invalid, but an address as 0.0.0.0 should be valid.

Iirc this function returns 1 if a valid address is matched, so I think the test seems to be checking that it's invalid (which looks right to me). Not sure if my intuition agrees with other implementations ATM tho
